chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from Muḥammad ibn Sinān, from Abī Khālid, from Abī Ḥamzah, from Abī Jaʿfar عليه السلام, who said:
Nothing cuts off the salat (prayer) except a nosebleed and rumbling in the belly, so deal with them promptly as much as you are able.

The proper way regarding these two reports is that we carry them upon a nosebleed whose sufferer needs to turn away from the qiblah or to speak. But when that is absent, then it does not cut off the salat (prayer), as has been detailed in the first two reports; and this is also indicated by further evidence.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةَ: salat (prayer), the ritual prayer whose continuity is being discussed
key_terms.الِانْصِرَافِ: turning away or departing, here from the qiblah during salat (prayer)
key_terms.الْبَطْنِ: the belly or abdomen, the place of the disturbance mentioned
key_terms.الْخَبَرَيْنِ: the two reports, referring to narrations being reconciled together
key_terms.الْقِبْلَةِ: the qiblah, the direction one must face in salat (prayer)
key_terms.الْكَلَامِ: speech, which may necessitate interruption of salat (prayer)
key_terms.رُعَافٌ: nosebleed, mentioned as a possible cause of interrupting salat (prayer)
key_terms.رِزٌّ: rumbling or disturbance in the belly

ai.seo_question: Does a nosebleed or stomach rumbling break salat (prayer) in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This report concerns the legal ruling on whether a nosebleed or abdominal rumbling interrupts salat (prayer). The text then reconciles the reports by explaining that interruption applies when the person must turn away from the qiblah or speak, while otherwise the salat (prayer) is not invalidated.
